before.content_html:
A Planet Becoming Urban

In 1800 just 3% of the world lived in cities. By 1900 the figure was 14%; in 2007 it crossed 50% for the first time; today it stands at over 56% and the UN forecasts 68% by 2050. Urbanisation — the rising share of people living in towns and cities — is the defining demographic shift of modern history. But the pace varies enormously: developed countries urbanised slowly between 1800 and 1950 and have plateaued; emerging countries are urbanising fastest right now; many developing countries still have the highest growth rates of all and will dominate the next century’s urban population.

Three Speeds of Urbanisation

In developed countries (UK, USA, Japan), urbanisation began with the Industrial Revolution — people moved from farms to factories in Manchester, Pittsburgh and Osaka. By 1950 most populations were already urban, and the trend slowed. The UK is now 84% urban; growth comes from international migration and small-town expansion rather than rural-to-urban movement. In emerging countries (China, India, Brazil), urbanisation is happening fast right now. China’s urban population grew from 26% in 1990 to 64% in 2024 — over half a billion people moved to cities in 30 years. In developing countries (Ethiopia, Bangladesh, DR Congo), cities are growing fast but most people are still rural; this is where the biggest urban explosion is still ahead. Africa’s urban population is projected to triple by 2050.

Key Fact

Today the world is over 56% urban. Developed countries (UK 84%) urbanised early and slow. Emerging countries (China 26% → 64% in 30 years) are urbanising fastest now. Developing countries (Ethiopia ~22%) face the biggest urban growth ahead.

Causes of Urbanisation

Urbanisation is driven by push and pull factors. Push factors include rural poverty, drought and crop failure, mechanisation that cuts farm jobs, conflict, and lack of services such as healthcare and secondary schools. Pull factors are the opposite: city jobs in industry and services, higher wages, hospitals and universities, electricity and clean water, and the perceived opportunity for a different life. Urbanisation also involves natural increase within cities — young migrants are typically of childbearing age, so birth rates spike. In emerging countries the pull factor is strongest where new manufacturing zones (Shenzhen, Bangalore) attract young workers in their millions.

Cities can grow faster than housing supply, leading to informal settlements (favelas in Rio, Dharavi in Mumbai) where over a billion people now live worldwide. Pressure on water, sewage and electricity grows; commuting times stretch. But urbanisation can also lift incomes — cities concentrate jobs, ideas and infrastructure efficiently. Shanghai grew from 7 million (1980) to 26 million (2024) and saw GDP per capita rise from $200 to over $25,000. The challenge for emerging-country governments is making the growth orderly — building affordable housing, transport and sanitation ahead of (or at least with) the migrants.

UK Distribution of Cities

The UK’s urban population sits in clear clusters. Greater London dominates with 9.7 million people — one in seven of the entire UK. The Midlands conurbation around Birmingham (4 million) was built on Industrial Revolution metalworking. The North-West conurbation around Manchester and Liverpool (2.8 million) grew from cotton mills and Atlantic shipping. The Yorkshire conurbation (Leeds, Sheffield, Bradford, 2 million) grew from wool, steel and coal. Scotland clusters in the Central Belt around Glasgow and Edinburgh (1.7 million). Outside these clusters, the UK is sparsely populated — Highland Scotland, Mid Wales and rural East Anglia have densities below 25 people/km2.

Why the UK’s Cities Sit Where They Do

UK city locations reflect history more than current geography. Cities grew where the Industrial Revolution found coal (the South Wales valleys, the Midlands, the North-East), iron ore (Sheffield), fast water for early mills (Pennine valleys), or port access for trade (Liverpool, Glasgow, Hull). London grew on a tidal Thames at the lowest crossable bridging point. Once industry collapsed in the 1970s and 80s — coal mines closed, Sheffield steel halved, Manchester cotton vanished — cities had to remake themselves around services, finance and digital industries. Some succeeded (Manchester through Media City and the universities); some still struggle (parts of South Wales and the North-East have not recovered the jobs they lost). The UK government’s ‘levelling up’ agenda from 2019 was an explicit response to this regional inequality.

Since the 1970s, many UK city dwellers have moved out to villages, market towns and the countryside — counter-urbanisation. Reasons: better roads (the M25, M6 and M62), electronic working (especially since 2020), perceived crime in cities, and rising house prices pushing families out. The Cotswolds, Lake District fringe and Cornwall have seen populations grow. The result is rural gentrification: services improve in lucky villages but house prices in places like Sandbanks (Dorset) reach London levels, pushing local young people out. Counter-urbanisation reshapes the UK pattern even as overall urbanisation continues globally.

Key Fact

The UK’s biggest conurbations — Greater London (9.7m), the West Midlands (4m), Greater Manchester/Merseyside (2.8m), Yorkshire (2m), the Central Belt (1.7m) — map onto Industrial Revolution coal, iron, textiles and ports.

lessons.title: A Major UK City: Site, Structure & Functions

before.content_html:
Birmingham as the UK Case Study

Edexcel asks for a detailed case study of one major UK city. We will use Birmingham — the UK’s second largest city, with 1.16 million people in the local authority and around 4 million across the wider West Midlands conurbation. Birmingham earns its place as a case study because it shows almost every classic urban story in one place: a manufacturing past, a service-economy reinvention, immigration, deindustrialisation, regeneration. Whether your answer is on site or structure or change, the figures sit ready to use.

Site & Situation

Geographers separate site from situation. Birmingham’s site sits on a low sandstone plateau roughly 140 m above sea level, well drained but with several streams (the Rea, the Tame) that powered early water mills. There is no major navigable river — an unusual feature for a major UK city — which is why canals later became so vital. Situation is about position relative to other places. Birmingham sits at the heart of England, almost equidistant from London, Manchester, Bristol and Liverpool. That central position made it the meeting-point of national road, canal and (later) rail networks. Today the M6, M42 and M5 motorways converge at Spaghetti Junction; New Street is the busiest railway station outside London.

Key Fact

Birmingham’s central location in England, plus access to nearby coalfields and the canal network linking it to the Mersey, Severn and Thames, made it the natural hub of the Industrial Revolution’s metalworking trade.

National, Regional & Global Context

In its national context, Birmingham is the second-largest UK city and a major financial, retail, education and convention hub. The 2022 Commonwealth Games and HS2 high-speed rail connection (under construction since 2019) reinforce its national role. Regionally, it anchors the West Midlands conurbation, including Wolverhampton, Walsall and Solihull. Around 25% of the UK’s manufacturing output still comes from this region. Globally, Birmingham connects through Birmingham Airport (12 million passengers a year), HSBC’s UK retail bank headquarters at Centenary Square, and a population that is now 51% non-white — one of the most diverse cities in Europe by share.

Connectivity

Connectivity is what makes a city function in the wider world. Birmingham’s connectivity has four layers. Road: the M6, M40, M5, M42 and A38(M) Aston Expressway converge here. Rail: New Street handles 53 million passenger journeys a year, with Moor Street and Snow Hill nearby. HS2 will cut London-Birmingham travel time to 49 minutes when fully open. Air: Birmingham Airport links to over 150 destinations. Digital: the city is part of the Midlands fibre-optic backbone and was an early UK 5G rollout site. Connectivity is one of Birmingham’s strongest assets and underpins everything from JLR car exports to the city’s university research economy.

Without a navigable river, Birmingham’s industrialists built their own water network: by 1830 the city had 174 km of canals — more than Venice. They linked to the Mersey for cotton imports, the Thames for London markets, and the Severn for coastal trade. Coal arrived from Cannock and the Black Country; finished metal goods left for the world. The canals were superseded by railways by the 1850s, but they explain why Birmingham could industrialise on a high, dry plateau without obvious water transport.

Urban Structure: From CBD to Fringe

Most UK cities — Birmingham included — show four concentric zones. The Central Business District (CBD) in central Birmingham covers New Street, Colmore Row, Brindleyplace and the Bullring. Buildings are tall (the Cube, 103 Colmore Row), land values are the highest in the city, and the use is offices, retail and conferences. The inner city (Aston, Sparkbrook, Handsworth) is older, mainly Victorian terraces with high population density, more deprivation but also strong community networks and a youthful population. The suburbs (Bournville, Edgbaston, Erdington) date from the late 19th and 20th centuries, with semi-detached and detached housing, gardens, parks, more car ownership. The urban-rural fringe (around Bromsgrove and Solihull) holds business parks, retail centres (Touchwood), the airport and farmland transitioning into commuter villages.

Functions Across the Zones

Each zone has different functions. The CBD’s function is commercial — banks, shops, hotels, conferences. The inner city’s function is mainly residential, increasingly mixed with start-ups in regenerated areas like Digbeth’s Custard Factory creative quarter. The suburbs are residential and educational — the University of Birmingham’s Edgbaston campus has 38,000 students. The fringe is industrial and commercial — logistics warehouses near the M42, JLR’s Solihull plant, the National Exhibition Centre and Birmingham Airport. Building age generally falls as you move outwards: CBD has the newest skyscrapers, inner city has the oldest housing, suburbs are mid-20th-century, the fringe is post-1980.

Older British cities show a paradox — the CBD usually has both the oldest historic buildings (the Town Hall, St Philip’s Cathedral) AND the newest skyscrapers, because central land is recycled most aggressively. The inner city is a band of mid-Victorian housing untouched since 1900. The suburbs grew between 1900 and 1970 with consistent semi-detached architecture. The fringe is dominated by post-1980 industrial sheds, commuter estates and out-of-town shopping. This pattern is not random: it reflects when each ring was built and how often each is redeveloped.

Key Fact

Birmingham’s four zones: CBD (Bullring, Brindleyplace — offices, retail), inner city (Aston, Sparkbrook — older housing, denser population), suburbs (Edgbaston, Bournville — family housing), urban-rural fringe (Solihull, NEC — airport, logistics, retail).
before.exam_tip_html: Edexcel will give you 12 marks across the ‘chosen UK city’ section if you can name and locate features. Always quote a specific Birmingham place name (Edgbaston, Brindleyplace, Solihull) and a figure (53 million rail journeys, 12 million airport passengers, 1.16 million city population). For 8-mark questions on site and situation, use both terms and show the difference: site = the physical ground; situation = position relative to other places. Sketch the four zones if there is space — examiners reward labelled diagrams.

lessons.title: Change & Inequality in a UK City

before.content_html:
A City in Constant Motion

Birmingham is the UK’s second-largest city, and like every major British city it has been redrawn over the past century by people moving in, jobs leaving and shopping habits changing. The Edexcel specification asks you to track those four changes — urbanisation, suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation and re-urbanisation — through one chosen UK city, then explain how migration and economic change have produced today’s patterns of inequality.

The Sequence of Urban Change in Birmingham

Birmingham urbanised explosively between 1801 and 1911, growing from 74,000 people to over half a million as the metalworking and small-arms trades drew workers in. From the 1950s, slum clearance and the building of the M5/M6 pushed families outwards into suburbs such as Solihull and Sutton Coldfield — classic suburbanisation. From the 1970s, counter-urbanisation took middle-income households even further out into Worcestershire and Staffordshire commuter villages. Since the early 2000s, regeneration of the Bullring, the Mailbox and Eastside has driven re-urbanisation: young professionals are returning to apartments in the city centre.

Key Fact

The four-stage sequence — urbanisation → suburbanisation → counter-urbanisation → re-urbanisation — can all be seen in Birmingham. The 2021 Census recorded a city population of 1.14 million, the largest since 1971.

Migration: National and International

Birmingham’s population is one of the most ethnically mixed in the UK. Post-war Commonwealth migration brought workers from the Caribbean, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh into inner-city wards such as Sparkbrook, Aston and Handsworth during the 1950s and 1960s. EU enlargement in 2004 added a wave of Polish and Romanian migrants. The 2021 Census shows that 51.4% of residents identify as a minority ethnic group, and around a quarter were born outside the UK. National migration is also strong: students from across the UK fill four large universities, and graduates often stay in the city centre after qualifying.

The impact of migration is uneven. Inner-city wards have a much younger age structure (median age around 29 in Sparkbrook) and higher demand for primary schools, mosques, temples and language services. Outer suburbs such as Sutton Coldfield are older (median age around 44) and need more care services and bus routes for the elderly. Housing pressure concentrates in inner wards where terraces are subdivided into multi-occupied flats.

Push factors include conflict, low wages and limited education in some sending countries. Pull factors include established family networks (chain migration into wards like Sparkhill), demand for low-cost labour in services and food processing, English-language universities, and HS2 construction jobs. Internal migration from the rest of the West Midlands is also important: people move into Birmingham for higher-skilled jobs in finance and law, then often move out again to suburban estates once they start a family.

Deindustrialisation and Economic Change

For a century Birmingham was Britain’s factory floor — cars at Longbridge, jewellery in the Jewellery Quarter, machine tools across the inner suburbs. Deindustrialisation hit hard from the 1970s onwards. Globalisation moved production to lower-wage countries; technological change reduced the workforce needed in surviving plants; container shipping and motorways allowed firms to decentralise to cheaper greenfield sites. The closure of MG Rover at Longbridge in 2005 alone cost roughly 6,000 direct jobs and another 12,000 in the supply chain.

The city has since shifted towards a service economy: business services, banking, higher education, conferencing and media. HSBC moved its UK retail bank headquarters to Centenary Square in 2018, and HS2’s Curzon Street terminus is anchoring further commercial development. But the new jobs are concentrated in the city centre — areas like Ladywood and Aston, which once depended on factory work, have struggled to replace it.

Inequality and Quality of Life

Economic change has widened the gap between Birmingham’s neighbourhoods. The Index of Multiple Deprivation places several inner wards (Ladywood, Lozells, Bordesley Green) among the 10% most deprived in England, while Sutton Four Oaks sits in the 20% least deprived. Male life expectancy ranges from 73 years in Ladywood to 82 in Sutton Coldfield — a nine-year gap inside one local authority. Child poverty in Ladywood reached around 47% in 2023, more than double the city average. Causes include long-term unemployment, lower-skilled service jobs, overcrowded housing and poorer air quality near the M6 and Spaghetti Junction.

Birmingham’s Central Business District lost ground in the 1980s and 1990s as out-of-town centres opened: Merry Hill at Brierley Hill (1985) and Touchwood at Solihull (2001) drew shoppers away with free parking and one-stop convenience. The CBD fought back with the rebuilt Bullring (2003) and Grand Central (2015), but online shopping has hit footfall again — Debenhams in the Bullring closed in 2021 and the former House of Fraser building on Corporation Street stands empty. The result is a more concentrated CBD focused on premium retail, leisure and food, with vacant smaller units on side streets.

Key Fact

Birmingham’s east-west inequality is sharp: male life expectancy is 73 in Ladywood versus 82 in Sutton Coldfield, and child poverty exceeds 45% in several inner wards. Deindustrialisation, migration patterns and retail decentralisation all helped produce that gap.

Strategies to Improve Quality of Life

The city council’s response combines several strands. Affordable housing schemes such as Perry Barr (originally built for the 2022 Commonwealth Games athletes’ village) are adding around 1,400 new homes. The Clean Air Zone introduced in 2021 charges older, polluting vehicles entering the city centre, cutting nitrogen-dioxide levels by an estimated 13% in the first year. Investment in education includes free school meals expansion and the new Curzon Investment Plan funding 500 apprenticeships in HS2-related construction. Recycling schemes, bus-route improvements and energy-efficient retrofits of council housing tackle environmental and cost-of-living pressures together. Critics argue the gains are uneven — the Clean Air Zone helps central wards more than outer ones — but the city’s footprint per resident is falling.
before.exam_tip_html: Edexcel A’s Paper 2 expects a named UK city throughout — if you write ‘in many UK cities’ you will lose marks. For 8-mark questions, build chains of reasoning: deindustrialisation → lost manufacturing jobs → lower household income in inner wards → poorer health outcomes. For 12-mark evaluations, weigh strategies against each other (affordable housing vs Clean Air Zone) and reach a justified conclusion. Always include at least two specific Birmingham statistics — examiners reward precise place knowledge over generic urban theory.

lessons.title: A Major City in a Developing or Emerging Country

before.content_html:
Mumbai: India’s Megacity

Mumbai is the financial capital of India and one of the largest cities in the world, with a metropolitan population of around 22 million in 2024. It is classed as an emerging country city, and the Edexcel specification expects you to know its site, structure, growth and challenges in detail. Studying one city in depth gives you the named places and statistics needed for 8- and 12-mark questions.

Site, Situation and Connectivity

Mumbai sits on a narrow peninsula on the west coast of India, with the Arabian Sea on three sides. The original site was seven small islands joined together by land reclamation between 1782 and 1845 — this geography squeezes a huge population into a thin north-south strip and explains why land prices in South Mumbai are among the highest in the world. Its situation is excellent: a deep natural harbour for shipping, a hinterland of cotton-growing Maharashtra, and connections to global markets through the world’s busiest container ports at Jawaharlal Nehru Port. Connectivity is supported by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, the Mumbai-Ahmedabad Highway, the new Mumbai Coastal Road, and the underground Mumbai Metro, with new lines opening through 2024.

Key Fact

Mumbai’s metropolitan population grew from around 8 million in 1981 to around 22 million in 2024. Drivers include rural-to-urban migration from drought-prone Maharashtra and Bihar, foreign direct investment in finance and Bollywood, and the deep natural harbour that made it India’s gateway to global trade.

Structure of the City

Mumbai’s structure is unusual because the peninsula forces it into long zones rather than concentric rings. The southern tip holds the historic Central Business District around Fort and Nariman Point, with British-era stone buildings, the Bombay Stock Exchange and corporate headquarters. The Bandra-Kurla Complex is a newer secondary CBD developed since the 1990s. North of the centre lie densely packed inner-city neighbourhoods of mid-rise housing, alongside major informal settlements such as Dharavi. Suburbs like Andheri and Borivali stretch up the peninsula, and an urban-rural fringe of mangrove forest, salt pans and the Sanjay Gandhi National Park pushes growth further inland on either side of the bay. Building age tells the story too: colonial Gothic in the south, art-deco from the 1930s along Marine Drive, glass towers in BKC, and self-built single-storey housing in the slums.

Natural increase is part of the story — many migrants are young adults of working age who go on to have families. But migration matters more. National migrants come from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar (poverty, low farm income), Maharashtra’s rural districts (drought and crop failure), and Kerala (skilled service workers). International migration is smaller but rising, especially from the Gulf, Africa and Bangladesh. Pull factors include construction jobs, domestic service in middle-class flats, the textile and pharmaceuticals industries, IT services in BKC, and the chance for work in the informal economy.

Inequality: Wealth and Poverty Side by Side

Mumbai contains both extreme wealth and extreme poverty within a few hundred metres. Antilia, the 27-storey private home of Mukesh Ambani in Altamount Road, is one of the most expensive houses in the world. A short distance away, Dharavi houses around 850,000 people in roughly 2.4 km² — one of Asia’s largest informal settlements. Quality-of-life indicators reflect the gap. Infant mortality in low-income wards is around 30 per 1,000, three times higher than in the affluent south. Around 41% of the city’s population lives in informal housing, often without legal land tenure or piped water. Reasons for the gap include shortage of formal housing, low rural incomes that drive migrants into self-built shelters, and a planning system that has long favoured high-end commercial development over affordable housing.

Challenges from Rapid Growth

Rapid urbanisation has produced four big challenges. Infrastructure is overstretched: only around 60% of households have a sewer connection, and electricity load-shedding still hits low-income areas. Housing supply lags far behind demand. Informal employment dominates — roughly half of Mumbai’s working population earns its income outside the formal economy, from rag-pickers and street vendors to home-based garment workers. And pollution has become severe: PM2.5 air-quality readings often exceed WHO guidelines tenfold during the dry season, and the Mithi River carries heavy industrial waste into Mahim Bay. Flooding adds a fifth pressure: monsoons in 2005 and again in 2021 paralysed the city when blocked drains overflowed.

Top-down strategies are led by central or state government. The Dharavi Redevelopment Project, restarted in 2023 by a consortium led by the Adani Group, plans to clear and rebuild the slum with high-rise flats, shops and infrastructure. The Mumbai Metro extensions, the Coastal Road, and the Mumbai Trans-Harbour Link (opened January 2024) all aim to ease congestion. Bottom-up approaches work with residents. The Slum Networking Project channels small grants to community groups for shared toilets, paving and water taps; the Society for the Promotion of Area Resource Centres (SPARC) helps residents form savings federations to negotiate with developers. Top-down can deliver scale; bottom-up keeps livelihoods intact and gives residents a voice.

Key Fact

Around 41% of Mumbai’s population lives in informal settlements, around half of all workers are in informal employment, only ~60% of households have sewer connections, and PM2.5 air pollution can reach ten times WHO guidelines. These four indicators capture the scale of the city’s urban challenge.

Government Policies and Quality of Life

The Maharashtra state government and the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation use a mix of strategies. Economically, special economic zones in BKC and Mahape attract IT and finance jobs that raise tax revenue for services. Socially, the Mid-Day Meal scheme provides hot lunches in 1,200 municipal schools, raising attendance and nutrition. Environmentally, the city has banned single-use plastics, expanded mangrove protection and restarted the Mithi River clean-up. Critics argue the gains are uneven — redevelopment can displace vulnerable residents, and air pollution still kills an estimated 25,000 people a year — but quality of life is rising on most indicators, with literacy at 89% and life expectancy now over 74.
before.exam_tip_html: Edexcel A asks for the same depth on your developing/emerging city as on your UK city. For 6-mark questions, give two developed challenges with named places (Dharavi, Mithi River) and a statistic each. For 8-mark questions, weigh top-down (Metro extensions, Dharavi Redevelopment) against bottom-up (SPARC, Slum Networking Project) and reach a judgement. Avoid generalising about ‘developing countries’ — examiners want Mumbai-specific evidence in every paragraph.

before.content_html:
What Does ‘Development’ Actually Mean?

Development is one of those words that sounds simple until you try to measure it. A century ago, geographers thought of development almost entirely as wealth: rich countries were ‘developed’, poor ones were not. Today, the word is far broader. Edexcel A asks you to think about development in three overlapping ways — economic, social and political — and to know the strengths and limits of the indicators used to measure each.

Economic Definitions

The classic economic measure is GDP per capita. It tells you, on average, how much income each person in a country produces in a year. In 2022 the UK’s GDP per capita was around $46,000 (US dollars, PPP-adjusted), Bangladesh’s was around $7,300 and Norway’s was around $82,000. GDP per capita is easy to compare across countries because the data is collected the same way everywhere, and it correlates well with formal job availability, infrastructure spending and tax revenue.

But GDP has serious blind spots. It is an average that ignores how income is distributed — a country with one billionaire and a million people in poverty can record the same GDP per capita as a country where everyone earns roughly the same. It misses unpaid work (childcare, subsistence farming) and the informal economy that may employ half of a city like Mumbai. It says nothing about whether the wealth is being used for hospitals or for personal jets. And it does not register the cost of environmental damage caused by economic activity.

Key Fact

GDP per capita is the most widely used economic measure of development, but it ignores income inequality, unpaid and informal work, environmental damage, and how money is spent. It is necessary but not sufficient.

Social and Composite Measures

Social measures look at how people actually live. Common indicators are life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy rate, mean years of schooling and access to clean water. To combine economic and social information into one number, the United Nations Development Programme created the Human Development Index (HDI) in 1990. HDI runs from 0 (worst) to 1 (best). The 2024 HDI report places Switzerland at 0.967, the UK at 0.940, India at 0.644 and Niger at 0.394. HDI is more nuanced than GDP because it captures health and education, but it still misses inequality between groups, environmental factors and political freedom.

The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a 0 to 1 scale (0 = perfect equality, 1 = one person owns everything). Slovenia is around 0.24, the UK around 0.35, the United States around 0.41 and South Africa around 0.63. The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) discounts the headline HDI to reflect uneven distribution. The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) counts the share of people deprived in education, health and living standards together — a sharper picture in countries where averages hide deep poverty. The Gender Inequality Index captures the gap between men and women in health, empowerment and the labour market. Geographers usually pick a small basket of these rather than rely on a single number.

Political Measures and Corruption

Political development is harder to measure but matters because the rules a country lives by determine whether economic growth turns into widespread benefits. Common indicators include the right to vote in fair elections, freedom of speech and the press, and indices of corruption. Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) scored Denmark 90/100 (least corrupt) in 2023, the UK 71, India 39 and Somalia 11 (most corrupt). Countries with persistently low CPI scores often see economic gains captured by elites and public services collapse, which slows broader development.

Wider Factors: Food, Water and Technology

Edexcel A also asks about food and water security, and technological access. Food security measures the calories and nutrition available, the share of children stunted by malnutrition (37% in some Sahel countries) and dependence on food imports. Water security tracks the share of households with safely managed drinking water (close to 100% in the UK, around 60% in India). Technology now matters too: mobile phone subscriptions per 100 people, broadband coverage and internet usage all shape opportunity. Cultural factors — gender roles, language access to global trade, religious freedoms — can speed up or hold back human development even when the economy grows.

Key Fact

Composite measures (HDI, IHDI, MPI), inequality measures (Gini), political measures (CPI) and security measures (food, water) capture parts of development that GDP cannot. The 2024 HDI ranks Switzerland top (0.967) and Niger bottom (0.394).

A single indicator gives a partial picture, so geographers combine them. Compare Saudi Arabia (high GDP per capita, around $59,000, but mid-range HDI of 0.875 and a low CPI of 52) with Costa Rica (lower GDP per capita, around $26,000, but a higher HDI of 0.806 relative to income and a CPI of 55). Saudi Arabia’s wealth is concentrated in oil; Costa Rica’s investment in health and education has stretched a smaller economy further. The same logic applies to ranking development within the UK — the South East scores higher than the North East on GDP and most social measures, but Scotland and Wales sometimes outperform on health spending or pre-school education.

Limits and Trade-Offs

No measure is perfect. Composite indices smooth over real differences inside countries: India’s national HDI hides huge gaps between Kerala and Bihar. Indices that depend on self-reported data (like the CPI) are subjective. And data quality is uneven: the World Bank itself warns that GDP figures for around 30 of its member states are based on outdated surveys. Most exam answers expect you to argue that no single number tells the whole story — the right approach is to triangulate two or three indicators and acknowledge what each one misses.
before.exam_tip_html: Edexcel A loves the question ‘assess the usefulness of one measure of development’. Always quote one strength and one weakness with a country example. For 8-mark questions, compare two indicators — e.g. argue that GDP and HDI together tell you more than either alone, then conclude. Memorise three or four named statistics (UK HDI 0.940, India HDI 0.644, Saudi GDP per capita ~$59,000) so you have specific evidence for any answer.

practice_questions.text:
Which measure combines income, life expectancy and years of schooling into a single 0-to-1 score?
A) GDP per capita
B) Gini coefficient
C) Human Development Index
D) Corruption Perceptions Index

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year, divided by its population, often adjusted for purchasing power parity. Secure: Total economic output divided by population. Developing: A measure of a country’s wealth. Emerging: Mentions money without precision.

practice_questions.text: Explain one limitation of GDP per capita as a measure of development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a clear limitation (ignores inequality / unpaid work / environmental damage / informal economy) and develops the consequence (e.g. a country with high GDP can still have poor average quality of life). Secure: Limitation named with linked impact. Developing: Limitation stated without development. Emerging: Vague comment on accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern shown by HDI in 2024.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names highest and lowest performers (Switzerland 0.967, Niger 0.394), notes the broad north-south split with North America, Western Europe and East Asia at the top, sub-Saharan Africa at the bottom, and identifies anomalies (oil-rich Gulf states). Secure: Three quantitative points with named regions. Developing: Two general points. Emerging: One vague trend.

practice_questions.text: Explain how political and economic measures of development can give different results.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points using examples — e.g. Saudi Arabia (high GDP, lower CPI), Costa Rica (lower GDP, similar CPI to UK), India (rising GDP, low CPI). Explains why oil wealth, corruption or political freedom can pull rankings apart. Secure: Two developed points with examples. Developing: Difference noted but examples thin. Emerging: General contrast only.

practice_questions.text: ‘A single indicator can never measure development accurately.’ Assess this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument for and against, considering GDP, HDI, Gini, CPI and food/water security with statistics (UK HDI 0.940, Norway GDP $82,000, etc.). Reaches a justified conclusion that triangulating measures is more reliable but a single composite (HDI) gets close. Secure: Both sides with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One-sided answer. Emerging: List of indicators without argument.

lessons.title: Uneven Global Development & Strategies to Address It

before.content_html:
A World That Is Not Flat

If you map global GDP per capita, the result is striking: a wide band of high-income countries across North America, Western Europe, the Gulf, East Asia and Australasia, and a wide band of low-income countries across sub-Saharan Africa, parts of South Asia and Central America. The gap between richest and poorest is huge — Norway’s GDP per capita is around 35 times that of Burundi. Geographers call this uneven development. The Edexcel A specification asks why those differences exist, what consequences they cause, and which strategies have been used to close the gap.

Physical Causes of Uneven Development

Physical geography is one starting point. Landlocked countries (Niger, Bolivia, Mongolia) trade more slowly than coastal ones because exporting goods costs more. Tropical climates spread diseases like malaria more easily, hurting the workforce; the World Health Organization estimates malaria still kills around 600,000 people a year. Drought-prone regions (the Sahel, north-east Brazil) struggle with food security. Tectonic and weather hazards — Haiti’s 2010 earthquake or repeated cyclones in Bangladesh — can wipe out years of investment. And uneven mineral wealth (oil in Norway and Saudi Arabia, copper in Chile) creates lasting differences when these resources are managed well or badly.

Key Fact

Physical (climate, hazards, landlockedness, resources), historic (colonialism, conflict) and economic (trade, debt, technology) causes interact to produce uneven development. Norway’s GDP per capita is roughly 35 times that of Burundi.

Historic and Economic Causes

History matters too. Colonialism reshaped the economies of much of Africa, Asia and the Americas to serve imperial powers, leaving newly independent countries with infrastructure designed for export rather than internal development. Trade rules still favour wealthier countries: rich-country tariffs on processed cocoa or cotton encourage poorer countries to export raw materials at lower prices. Debt repayment can absorb a fifth or more of national income, leaving little for hospitals or schools. Conflict erases progress — the World Bank estimates Yemen has lost almost half its GDP since 2015. Within the UK, history echoes too: the North-South divide owes much to the location of coalfields and ports two centuries ago.

Consequences of Uneven Development

The consequences run through every part of life. In housing, around 1.1 billion people worldwide live in informal settlements (UN-Habitat, 2024). In health, life expectancy ranges from 84 years in Japan to 53 in the Central African Republic. In education, secondary school enrolment is over 95% in OECD countries but below 40% in parts of the Sahel. In employment, formal jobs are concentrated in richer countries while two billion people work in the informal economy. In food and water security, around 735 million people went hungry in 2023 according to the UN, mostly in low-income countries. Technology amplifies the gap: 4G coverage is near-universal in Western Europe but only around 30% in rural sub-Saharan Africa, which limits the chance to leapfrog into mobile banking, e-learning and online business.

Uneven development is not only a global story. The UK’s GDP per capita varies from around £57,000 in inner London to £19,000 in parts of Cornwall and the North East. Healthy life expectancy is around 65 in the South East but as low as 58 in Glasgow City. Causes include the long shadow of deindustrialisation in the Midlands and the North, concentration of finance and high-skilled service jobs in London, and historic underinvestment in northern transport. The Levelling Up White Paper (2022) and the cancelled HS2 northern leg (2023) show how policy choices can either narrow or widen these gaps.

International Strategies: Aid and Agreements

Many strategies aim to reduce uneven development. International aid can be bilateral (one government to another), multilateral (through organisations like the World Bank or UN) or non-governmental (charities such as Oxfam). The UK aid budget was £15.4 billion in 2023, though the share of national income spent on aid was cut from 0.7% to 0.5% in 2021. Inter-governmental agreements include the UN Sustainable Development Goals (17 targets to 2030), the Paris Climate Agreement (2015) and trade-policy steps like the EU’s Everything But Arms scheme, which removes tariffs on most exports from Least Developed Countries. Critics argue some aid creates dependency, especially when it props up bad governance, but well-designed aid can save lives quickly — the GAVI vaccine alliance has helped immunise over a billion children since 2000.

Key Fact

Top-down development is decided centrally by governments or large organisations and tends to be large-scale (dams, highways, vaccine programmes). Bottom-up development is led by communities and tends to be small-scale (water pumps, micro-loans, schools).

Top-Down Strategies

Top-down approaches use scale and central planning. Examples include the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, the Three Gorges Dam in China, and the World Bank’s funding of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad rail corridor. Strengths: they can deliver infrastructure quickly, attract private investment, and unlock economies of scale. Weaknesses: they can ignore local knowledge, displace residents (the Three Gorges Dam moved 1.3 million people), and saddle countries with debt if benefits don’t match the cost. Transnational corporations (TNCs) can act top-down too — Shell’s investments in the Niger Delta have brought tax income but caused serious environmental damage.

Bottom-Up Strategies

Bottom-up approaches start with the community. Micro-loans from groups like the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh have allowed millions of women to start businesses since the 1980s. Practical Action’s rope pumps in Kenya are made by local welders, fixed by villagers and cost a tenth of an imported diesel pump. WaterAid’s borehole programmes are designed jointly with the village water committee. Strengths: low cost, appropriate technology, builds local skills, sustains itself after donors leave. Weaknesses: small scale, slow to spread, and harder to coordinate across regions. Many geographers argue the most effective programmes pair the two — large infrastructure provides the backbone, community schemes deliver the last mile.

Imagine two villages without piped water. The top-down option is a $200 million regional pipeline funded by a World Bank loan: clean water at every tap within four years, but a debt that takes 20 years to pay off and limited say for villagers in where the pipes run. The bottom-up option is a community well drilled with $5,000 of NGO support, repaired by a trained villager, plus a savings group for hygiene products: clean water within months for one village only, but at a fraction of the cost and with skills that stay in the community. The choice depends on the scale of the problem, the strength of local institutions and how much risk the country can absorb.

knowledge_checks.q: Which physical factor commonly slows development in landlocked countries?
options: Higher trade costs and slower exports

knowledge_checks.q: Which agreement set 17 international targets for development by 2030?
The Grameen Bank in Bangladesh became famous for offering _____-loans to women setting up small businesses.
The Three Gorges Dam in China displaced an estimated _____ million people.
Match each example to its development approach.

lessons.title: Development in a Developing or Emerging Country

before.content_html:
India: An Emerging Country in Detail

India is the world’s most populous country, with around 1.43 billion people in 2024, and the fifth-largest economy. It is classed as an emerging country. The Edexcel A specification asks for a country case study covering location, economic change, geopolitics and the impacts of rapid development. India fits well because the changes are recent, well-documented and very uneven inside the country.

Location and Context

India sits in South Asia, bordered by Pakistan to the west, China and Nepal to the north, Bangladesh and Myanmar to the east, and the Indian Ocean to the south. Its position links the Middle Eastern oil and gas markets with the East Asian manufacturing belt, and the Mumbai-Singapore shipping lanes carry around a third of global trade. Politically, India is the world’s largest democracy, a member of the BRICS group and the G20, with diaspora communities of over 18 million in the UK, the United States and the Gulf. Religiously and culturally it is mostly Hindu (around 80%) but contains the world’s second-largest Muslim population. Environmentally, the Himalayas in the north, the Thar Desert in the west, the Ganges plain in the centre and the rainforests of Kerala in the south create huge regional contrasts.

Key Fact

India had a population of around 1.43 billion in 2024, an HDI of 0.644, and is the world’s fifth-largest economy. It borders Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and is a member of BRICS and the G20.

Core and Periphery: Uneven Development Within India

Development is very uneven across India. Coastal and southern states (Kerala HDI ~0.781, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra) form the core. Inland and northern states (Bihar HDI ~0.574, Jharkhand, Odisha) form the periphery. Reasons include access to ports for trade, longer histories of education investment (Kerala has had near-universal literacy since the 1990s), better infrastructure and stronger state governance. Bihar still has a child stunting rate of around 40% and a literacy rate of 70%, compared with Kerala’s 96%. The Modi government’s ‘Aspirational Districts’ programme targets the 112 weakest districts — mostly in the periphery — with health and education funding.

Economic Change Across the Sectors

India’s economy has shifted dramatically. In 1991, the primary sector (mostly agriculture) contributed about 30% of GDP; today it is around 17%, although it still employs around 42% of the workforce. The secondary sector (manufacturing) grew rapidly after 1991 economic reforms; sectors like pharmaceuticals (Cipla, Sun Pharma) and automotive (Tata Motors, Maruti Suzuki) are now world leaders. The tertiary sector (services) is the largest, contributing around 55% of GDP — finance, retail, healthcare, tourism. The quaternary sector (knowledge industries: IT, software, research) has exploded around Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune. Companies like Infosys and TCS make India a global IT services hub, employing more than 5 million people. The Modi government’s ‘Make in India’ initiative (launched 2014) aims to raise manufacturing’s share of GDP towards 25%.

India’s exports were worth around $770 billion in 2023, dominated by refined petroleum, IT services, gems and pharmaceuticals. Top trading partners are the United States, China and the United Arab Emirates. India once received large amounts of overseas aid; today it gives more than it receives, with $36 billion of foreign direct investment flowing in during 2023 from companies such as Apple (now manufacturing iPhones in Tamil Nadu) and Foxconn. Public investment by the state remains important — $26 billion for renewable energy and railway upgrades in 2023 — but private investment by TNCs is increasingly setting the pace. The shifting balance is part of India’s emergence: government provides infrastructure, corporations provide jobs.

Population, Society and Inequality

India’s population pyramid has narrowed at the base over the past 30 years. Total fertility has fallen from around 4.5 children per woman in 1990 to around 2.0 in 2023, slightly below replacement. Life expectancy rose from 58 in 1990 to 70 in 2023. The middle class has grown to around 430 million, fuelling demand for cars, apartments and tertiary education. But inequality has widened: the top 10% of earners take home around 57% of national income, while around 130 million people still live below the international extreme-poverty line. Female participation in the labour force is around 27% — one of the lowest in Asia — held back by social expectations, safety concerns and limited childcare. Education improvements (the Right to Education Act, 2009) have raised primary enrolment to over 95%, but secondary completion is still under 60%.

Geopolitics and Technology

India’s development is shaped by its neighbours and its global role. Long-running territorial disputes with Pakistan over Kashmir and with China over Ladakh have led to military skirmishes (the 2020 Galwan Valley clash) that absorb large defence budgets — around 2.5% of GDP. Cooperation agreements include the Quad (with the United States, Japan and Australia) and a free-trade pact with the UAE (2022). Technology has been transformational: the Aadhaar biometric identity scheme has enrolled over 1.3 billion people, allowing direct cash transfers and cutting fraud in welfare schemes. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed over 14 billion transactions in October 2024 alone, leapfrogging credit cards. Mobile internet now reaches 850 million Indians, although rural areas and women still lag.

Key Fact

Rapid development has produced positives (life expectancy +12 years since 1990, IT services hub, growing middle class) and negatives (top 10% earn 57% of income, child stunting 35% nationally, Delhi air pollution among the worst in the world).

Positive and Negative Impacts of Rapid Development

The positives are real. Hundreds of millions have been lifted out of extreme poverty since the 1990s. The economy is forecast to overtake Germany’s by 2027. Renewable energy capacity (solar especially) has grown from almost nothing to 73 GW in 2024, on track for 500 GW by 2030. The negatives are equally real. Air pollution kills around 1.7 million people a year, with Delhi’s PM2.5 frequently more than 15 times the WHO limit. Groundwater depletion in Punjab threatens long-term food security. Caste and gender inequalities still concentrate wealth in particular groups. The Indian government’s response includes the National Clean Air Programme (target: cut particulate pollution 40% by 2026), the Swachh Bharat sanitation drive (over 110 million toilets built since 2014) and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana housing scheme (delivering over 4 million urban houses for the poor by 2024).

Geographers debate whether India’s government can manage growth without locking in environmental damage and inequality. Top-down megaprojects (Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor, Solar Park at Bhadla in Rajasthan) deliver scale; bottom-up schemes (the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, which guarantees 100 days’ paid work a year for poor rural households) deliver fairness. The most effective response combines them — using megaproject tax revenue to fund welfare. The country’s commitments at COP26 (net zero by 2070) and the Lifestyle for Environment movement add an environmental dimension that earlier development models lacked.
before.exam_tip_html: India questions on Edexcel A reward precise place knowledge. Memorise three positive impacts (life expectancy gain, renewable capacity, middle class size) and three negative impacts (Delhi air pollution, top 10% income share, female labour participation) with statistics. For 12-mark evaluations, structure as positive impacts → negative impacts → how the government is responding → justified judgement. Always quote two named places (e.g. Bengaluru IT, Bihar core/periphery) so the answer is clearly about India and not generic.

practice_questions.text:
Roughly what was India’s population in 2024?
A) 0.5 billion
B) 1.0 billion
C) 1.43 billion
D) 2.5 billion
Name two sectors of the Indian economy that have grown rapidly since 1991.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear sectors named with brief specificity (e.g. tertiary services, quaternary IT and software, manufacturing such as automotive or pharmaceuticals). Secure: Two sectors named. Developing: One sector named. Emerging: General reference to industry.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason for uneven development within India.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a clear reason (port access for southern states / longer history of education in Kerala / weaker governance in Bihar / climate-related agricultural difference) with chain of reasoning — e.g. Kerala’s long investment in literacy enabled a service-sector workforce, raising HDI to 0.781. Secure: Reason and one developed link. Developing: Reason stated without development. Emerging: General comment.

practice_questions.text: Describe how India’s population structure has changed over the last 30 years.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names quantitative changes — fertility from ~4.5 (1990) to ~2.0 (2023), life expectancy from 58 to 70, narrower base of population pyramid, growing middle class (~430 million). Secure: Three changes with one statistic. Developing: General trend without numbers. Emerging: One change only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how geopolitics has affected India’s development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points covering territorial disputes (Kashmir, Ladakh, Galwan Valley 2020), defence spending (~2.5% of GDP), trade agreements (UAE 2022, Quad alliance), and impact on foreign investment, with named examples and a clear linked impact. Secure: Two developed points. Developing: One point with example. Emerging: General comment on neighbours.

practice_questions.text: ‘The benefits of India’s rapid development outweigh the costs.’ Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument balancing positives (poverty reduction, life expectancy +12 years, renewables 73 GW, IT services hub) against negatives (top 10% earn 57% of income, Delhi air pollution, groundwater depletion, female labour participation 27%) with chains of reasoning, named places and a justified judgement. Secure: Both sides with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One-sided answer. Emerging: List of impacts only.

before.content_html:
What Counts as a Natural Resource?

A natural resource is anything in the physical environment that can be used to meet human needs — food from the soil, energy from sunlight, fish from the sea, iron from the rocks. Geographers classify resources in two ways. First, by whether they are living: biotic resources come from living things, while abiotic resources come from the non-living world. Second, by whether they replace themselves: renewable resources can be used repeatedly if managed well; non-renewable resources are finite. Wind is renewable and abiotic; cod is renewable but biotic (if not over-fished); coal is non-renewable and abiotic.

How Humans Exploit the Environment

Three big resources — food, water and energy — drive most exploitation. Fishing fleets harvest 90 million tonnes of marine fish per year, with around a third of stocks now over-fished. Farming covers around 38% of the Earth’s land surface and uses around 70% of fresh water withdrawn worldwide. Fossil-fuel extraction continues at scale: around 4.5 billion tonnes of crude oil and 8 billion tonnes of coal a year. Deforestation clears around 10 million hectares of forest every year, much of it tropical. Each form of exploitation changes the place where it happens. Overfishing collapses food chains; intensive farming erodes soil and depletes aquifers; mining and drilling pollute air and water; deforestation removes habitat and releases stored carbon.

Key Fact

Resource exploitation causes reduced biodiversity (Amazon deforestation around 10 million hectares a year globally), soil erosion (intensive farming in East Anglia), and reduced water and air quality (PM2.5 hotspots over the Indo-Gangetic plain).

Global Distribution of Key Resources

Resources are unevenly distributed because geology, climate and land cover vary. Soil and agriculture concentrate in the world’s great river basins (Mississippi, Ganges, Indus, Nile) and in temperate plains (Ukraine, the US Midwest, Argentina’s pampas). Forestry depends on biome: the boreal forests of Russia and Canada and the tropical rainforests of the Amazon and Congo basins are the largest stores. Fossil fuels are tied to ancient sedimentary basins: oil in the Middle East (Saudi Arabia, Iran), the Gulf of Mexico, and Russia; coal in China, the US, India and Australia; natural gas in Russia, Iran and the United States. Water supply follows precipitation patterns: tropical rainforests, monsoon Asia and equatorial Africa receive most rain, while subtropical deserts (Sahara, Arabian Peninsula, Australia’s outback) face chronic shortage. Rocks and minerals follow geology: copper in the Andes, iron ore in Western Australia, lithium in the ‘triangle’ of Bolivia, Chile and Argentina.

UK Resource Distribution

The UK’s smaller landscape is also unevenly resourced. Soil and agriculture: rich loamy soils in East Anglia and the Vale of York support cereals; Welsh and Scottish uplands carry sheep and beef cattle. Forestry: Sitka spruce plantations cover around 13% of the UK; the largest blocks are in Galloway and the Kielder Forest in Northumberland. Fossil fuels: North Sea oil and gas (mostly off the coasts of Aberdeen and East Anglia) supply around 30% of UK gas demand, although output has fallen since the late 1990s. Coal still exists in disused fields in Yorkshire and Wales but commercial production has effectively ended. Water supply: Western and northern uplands (Lake District, Welsh hills, Scottish Highlands) receive around 2,000 mm rainfall a year, while East Anglia receives around 600 mm and depends on transfers and aquifers. Rock and minerals: granite from Cornwall and Aberdeenshire, limestone in the Pennines, china clay in St Austell, and small reserves of tin, lithium and tungsten.

Prevailing south-westerly winds carry moist Atlantic air over the UK. When this air meets uplands such as Snowdonia, the Lake District and the Highlands it is forced upwards, cools, and releases its rain (relief rainfall). By the time the air reaches the lowlands of the south-east it has already lost most of its moisture. The result is a stark gradient: Borrowdale in Cumbria averages over 3,300 mm a year (the wettest place in England) while London averages around 600 mm. This is why the UK as a whole has plenty of water but moves it through schemes like the Kielder Reservoir transfer.

Patterns of Consumption

Consumption is also uneven, but not in the same way as supply. Wealthy countries consume far more energy and food per person than poorer countries even when they have less raw resource. The average UK resident consumes around 2,800 kg of oil-equivalent energy a year; the average Bangladeshi consumes around 270 kg. The average UK resident eats around 80 kg of meat a year; the average Indian eats around 4 kg. Water consumption follows wealth too — an average North American uses around 200 litres a day for domestic purposes, an average Sub-Saharan African about 20 litres. Globalisation now blurs these patterns: a UK consumer drinking Kenyan coffee or eating Spanish strawberries is using virtual water and energy from another part of the world. Around 70% of the EU’s overall ‘water footprint’ comes from goods imported from beyond its borders.

Key Fact

Wealth, not just supply, drives consumption: the UK uses around ten times the energy per person of Bangladesh, and globalisation hides much of that consumption inside imported food and goods.

Why Distribution and Exploitation Matter

Distribution and consumption are connected. Countries with abundant resources but small populations (Norway’s oil, Saudi Arabia’s oil) export them to populous, resource-poor countries. The result is geopolitical leverage — Russia’s gas exports gave it political influence over European energy security until 2022. Resource exploitation reshapes the host place: oil revenue built Dubai’s skyline but groundwater abstraction lowered the city’s aquifer. Decisions made in cities far from the resource often determine its fate. Recognising the global pattern is the first step in the rest of the topic, where you will look at energy and water management in detail.

Choropleth maps colour countries by a value (say, energy consumption per capita). Read the legend first — bands are usually quintiles. Then describe with PEEL: Pattern (where is the highest band concentrated?), Exception (which country breaks the pattern?), Explain (what physical or human factor causes that?), Link (how does it connect to another map you’ve seen?). Edexcel often pairs a consumption map with a population map and asks you to spot mismatches between supply and demand.

before.content_html:
Why Energy Management Matters

Every economy runs on energy. The challenge for governments is to keep supply secure, affordable and clean enough to avoid catastrophic climate change. The Edexcel A specification asks you to know how energy resources are classified, how the UK’s energy mix compares with other countries, why demand has changed, and how managers can make energy use more sustainable through both top-down and bottom-up strategies.

Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Resources

Energy resources fall into two families. Renewable sources include hydroelectric power (HEP), wind, solar, geothermal and tidal. Non-renewable sources include coal, oil, natural gas and uranium (used in nuclear fission). Each has trade-offs. Coal is cheap and abundant but produces around 0.95 kg of CO₂ per kWh of electricity — roughly twice that of natural gas and far more than wind or solar. Wind power is clean but variable; solar is clean and falling fast in cost (around an 89% drop since 2010) but doesn’t work at night; nuclear delivers steady low-carbon power but creates radioactive waste that needs storing for thousands of years.

Key Fact

The UK electricity mix in 2023 was roughly: gas 32%, wind 29%, nuclear 14%, biomass 5%, solar 5%, imports 11% and coal less than 2%. Renewables and low-carbon together provided over half of UK electricity for the first time.

The UK’s Energy Mix in Detail

The UK has decarbonised faster than most large economies. In 1990, coal generated around 65% of UK electricity; in 2023, less than 2%. The last UK coal-fired power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in September 2024, ending more than a century of coal generation. Natural gas has filled some of the gap, and offshore wind has expanded enormously: Hornsea 2 off the Yorkshire coast, completed 2022, is currently the world’s largest operating offshore wind farm at 1.32 GW. Nuclear capacity has fallen as older stations close, but Hinkley Point C in Somerset is set to add 3.2 GW from 2027 (delayed from 2025). Solar farms are growing on lower-quality farmland in the south. Biomass at Drax in Yorkshire burns wood pellets imported mainly from North America.

Why Global Energy Mixes Differ

No two countries share the same mix. Norway runs on around 92% hydroelectric power thanks to high mountains and heavy rainfall. France generates around 65% of electricity from nuclear, a deliberate post-1970s policy. China still relies on coal for around 60% of electricity, despite leading the world in solar manufacturing. Saudi Arabia burns oil and gas because it has plenty of both. Three factors shape the mix: population (size of total demand), wealth (capacity to invest in costly infrastructure) and the natural availability of resources. Policy choices matter too — Germany shut its nuclear plants after the Fukushima accident in 2011, while the UK kept its open.

Three drivers explain rising demand since 1924. Population: the world has gone from around 2 billion to over 8 billion, multiplying total need. Wealth: GDP per capita has grown roughly seven-fold globally, so households heat bigger homes, drive cars and run more devices. Technology: industrial automation, data centres, electric heating and electric vehicles all draw far more power than the simpler economies of a century ago. Together these mean the world used around 25 times more primary energy in 2023 than in 1924, even though the energy intensity (energy per dollar of GDP) has actually fallen with efficiency improvements.

Impacts of Energy Production

Both renewable and non-renewable production has impacts. Coal mining scars landscapes, releases methane and pollutes water; the Aberfan tip disaster (1966) killed 144 people, mostly children, when coal-mining waste collapsed onto a school. Oil drilling carries spill risks — the Deepwater Horizon spill (2010) released 4.9 million barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico. Natural-gas fracking can resolve shortages but has been linked to small earthquakes and groundwater pollution; UK fracking near Blackpool was paused in 2019 after a 2.9 magnitude tremor. Renewables have impacts too: hydroelectric dams flood valleys (Three Gorges displaced 1.3 million people in China); wind farms can disrupt bird flight paths and concern coastal residents about views; solar farms occupy farmland; biomass at Drax has been criticised for the carbon footprint of shipping wood pellets across the Atlantic.

Key Fact

Sustainable energy management combines top-down (Hinkley Point C nuclear, the offshore wind expansion, Contracts for Difference) with bottom-up schemes (community solar, household insulation grants, electric-vehicle subsidies).

Stakeholders and Their Views

Energy decisions involve many stakeholders. Individuals weigh up cost, comfort and the environment when choosing a heating system. Businesses lobby for stable energy prices — the chemicals and steel sectors face huge gas bills. Local authorities campaign about visual impact and air quality. Governments balance energy security, jobs, climate targets and consumer bills. NGOs like Greenpeace push for faster decarbonisation, while organisations like the Confederation of British Industry lobby for cheaper power. The result is rarely consensus — but the UK’s legally binding 2050 net-zero target (passed by Parliament in June 2019) gives a clear long-term direction even when short-term arguments rage.

Sustainable Energy in a Developed and Emerging Country

The UK’s strategy combines several elements. Top-down: contracts that guarantee renewable producers a price (Contracts for Difference) have driven down offshore wind costs by around 70% since 2014. Hinkley Point C, the first new UK nuclear station in a generation, is under construction. The government plans to ban new petrol and diesel cars by 2035. Bottom-up: the Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants £7,500 toward heat pumps, the Smart Export Guarantee pays households for surplus solar power, and community energy co-operatives like Bath & West Community Energy own and run local solar farms. Compare with India: the Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan covers 14,000 acres and produces 2.25 GW of solar power; the Indian government’s target is 500 GW of renewable capacity by 2030; villages without grid electricity are leapfrogging straight to solar mini-grids supported by SELCO and other social enterprises. Both countries combine megaprojects with smaller community schemes, but India is electrifying for the first time, while the UK is replacing existing infrastructure.

A carbon footprint is the total CO₂ equivalent emissions caused by an individual, company or country. The average UK resident emits around 4.7 tonnes a year (2023), down from 9 tonnes in 1990. The average Indian emits around 1.9 tonnes; the average American around 14.7 tonnes. Households can cut their footprint by switching to a heat pump, insulating, eating less red meat and flying less. Edexcel may ask you to calculate or compare footprints — expect a basic table or formula. The point is that energy choice and lifestyle together determine carbon impact.

before.content_html:
Why Water Is Unevenly Shared

Although Earth’s surface is mostly water, only about 2.5% of it is fresh, and most of that is locked in glaciers or buried underground. The amount of freshwater a country can actually use depends on rainfall, geology and the technology to capture and clean it. The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Iceland have so much water they barely measure it; Saudi Arabia, parts of north Africa and inland Australia have almost none. Around 2 billion people live in countries where water demand exceeds reliable supply.

Key Fact

A water surplus exists where rainfall and stored water exceed demand — e.g. Scotland, the Congo Basin. A water deficit exists where demand outstrips supply — e.g. Egypt, south-east England in dry summers, the Sahel.

How Demand Has Changed in 50 Years

Global water use has roughly doubled since 1975. Three drivers explain almost all of it. Population growth — the world has gone from 4 billion to over 8 billion — means more drinking, washing and sanitation. Rising affluence brings power showers, dishwashers, swimming pools and meat-heavy diets that need huge volumes of water to grow grain for livestock. Industrialisation in countries such as China and India has raised factory and power-station demand sharply. Meanwhile, supply has not kept pace: aquifers are being pumped faster than rain replaces them, and climate change is lengthening dry seasons in regions that were already short.

Who Uses What — Developed vs Developing

Globally, agricultural water use takes about 70% of all freshwater. But the share differs sharply by income. In developing and emerging countries (e.g. India, Pakistan, Egypt) farming can take 80–90% of water because irrigation is essential to feed growing populations and food exports earn foreign currency. Industry and domestic use are small in comparison. In developed countries (e.g. the UK, Germany), domestic use rises to around 20% and industry to 30–40%, while farming falls to roughly 10% because food is often imported. So a wealthy household uses far more water at home, but a developing country uses far more in total because of irrigation.

The UK looks wet, but supply and demand are mismatched. Most rain falls in the north and west (Scotland, the Lake District, Wales) while most people live in the dry south and east (London, Cambridge, Essex). Summers concentrate demand — gardens, tourism, irrigation — just when rivers run lowest. Around 20% of treated water leaks out of an ageing Victorian pipe network before it reaches a tap; in 2024 Thames Water alone leaked over 570 million litres a day. The Environment Agency warns parts of south-east England could face serious shortages by 2050 without new reservoirs and transfer schemes.

Water Problems in Emerging & Developing Countries

In poorer countries the issue is rarely just rainfall. Many people lack access to treated water: in 2023 around 2.2 billion people had no safely managed drinking water at home. Rivers are often polluted by untreated sewage, factory waste or fertiliser run-off — the Yamuna in Delhi and the Ganges below Kanpur are textbook cases. Annual rainfall can also be low or unreliable: the Sahel has seen rainfall fall by around 20% since 1970. The result is widespread waterborne disease — cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea kill around 500,000 children under five each year, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.

Stakeholders Disagree About Water

Stakeholders rarely share the same view. Individuals tend to want cheap, plentiful water on demand and resent meters or hosepipe bans. Farmers and businesses push for licences to abstract from rivers and aquifers. Water companies — private in England, public elsewhere — have to balance shareholder profit, fines for leaks and pressure to invest in new pipes. Environmental groups argue rivers need a minimum flow for fish and wetlands. Governments set the rules, and may face the political cost of price rises or hosepipe bans. The London Pollard Switch Off campaign and Cape Town’s 2018 ‘Day Zero’ crisis both showed how quickly stakeholder conflict erupts when supply tightens.

Technology: Desalination & Beyond

Desalination turns seawater into freshwater by reverse osmosis or by boiling and condensing. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates rely on desalination for over half of their drinking water; Israel covers around 85% of household demand from five Mediterranean plants. The advantage is unlimited raw material — the sea. The drawbacks are heavy energy use (so often fossil-fuel-powered), salty brine discharged back into coastal waters, and high upfront cost. London’s Beckton plant, opened in 2010, was built as an emergency back-up rather than everyday supply for these reasons.

Singapore (developed) imports water from Malaysia but is closing the gap with the ‘Four National Taps’ strategy: local catchment, imports, NEWater (purified recycled wastewater) and desalination. NEWater now meets up to 40% of demand and is forecast to reach 55% by 2060. Tariffs rise sharply with use, so households pay more once they cross 40 m3/month, encouraging conservation. Wakal River Basin, Rajasthan (developing) has used WaterAid bottom-up projects to build small earth dams and stone johads that catch monsoon run-off, recharging village wells. Costs are low, communities maintain the structures, and groundwater levels have risen 5–10 m in the most successful villages. Both schemes are sustainable because they meet present demand without ruining future supply.

Key Fact

Sustainable water management combines top-down projects (Singapore’s Four National Taps, UK reservoirs and transfers) with bottom-up projects (rainwater harvesting in Rajasthan, hand-dug johads). Both must balance supply, demand and environment.
